newsitem.title: USA: U.S. mall REITs look to grow despite consolidation.
newsitem.headline: U.S. mall REITs look to grow despite consolidation.

text.p: Some of the major publicly-traded owners of shopping malls in the United States are looking to build even more malls.

But at the same time, these real estate investment trusts also expect consolidation in the mall industry, with some predicting that about 20 percent of the existing malls could fail in the next several years.
The rationale for this dichotomy is changing demographics, making new areas attractive for mall development while other areas cannot support the malls they have.

"I absolutely believe this is a very fragmented industry," said Robert Taubman, chief executive of Taubman Centers Inc, a Michigan-based REIT that owns 20 regional and super regional shopping centers.
Noting that there are more than 2,000 malls in the country, Taubman said many of those will not be around in the next several years.
"I've said publicly 500 will not survive," Taubman told a panel at a National Association of Real Estate Investment Trusts forum here.
But Taubman also said his company would like to build a mall every year, as others are also looking to build.

"New opportunities become available as demographics change and people move around," said Matthew Dominski, chief executive of Chicago-based Urban Shopping Centers Inc, which manages about 55-million square feet in 27 states and the District of Columbia. Dominski said Urban's goal is to develop a new property once every 18 months to two years.
"At the end of the day, this is an organic, living business," Taubman said. "This business takes more management than I think any other real estate business."

The REIT owners also said they expect to see more buyouts of smaller, private mall operators, though there was disagreement over whether there will be more mergers and acquisitions among public REITs.

"I don't see any compelling reasons for any (mergers and acquisitions) within the group that's public today," said Arthur Coppola, chief executive of Santa Monica, California-based Macerich Co, which has ownership interest in 18 malls and three community shopping centers.
He argued that the public companies are large enough that they don't need to merge to get lower costs of capital or better marketing efficiencies.
But others argued that then REITs still are not large enough to have the liquidity to attract some large investors.

"I think bigger will be better in the market, for exactly the liquidity reasons that people talked about," said Lee Schalop, equity analyst at J.P. Morgan Securities Inc. "Investors have interest in real estate but can't take reasonable-sized positions and so we're definitely going to see more companies get together."
